Observations on Visually Similar CIFAR-10 Classes (Task A1.2)

Inspecting the 32×32 RGB thumbnails above highlights why several class pairs are particularly challenging for a classifier: 1. Cat (Class 3) vs Dog (Class 5): Both are small domestic quadrupeds photographed indoors or on grass with overlapping fur colours, similar head-to-body proportions, and pointed/floppy ear contours that blur into only a few pixels at 32×32 resolution. 2. Automobile (Class 1) vs Truck (Class 9): Both share metallic bodies, windshields, headlights, rubber tyres, and asphalt road backgrounds. At 32×32 resolution, a pickup truck or SUV cab looks nearly identical to a sedan. 3. Deer (Class 4) vs Horse (Class 7) & Bird (Class 2) vs Airplane (Class 0): Deer and horses share brown coats and grassy woodland backgrounds, while birds in flight against blue skies share silhouette geometry with distant airplanes.

WHY Normalise Pixel Intensities to [0, 1]? (Task A1.3)

  • Faster & More Stable Gradient Descent Convergence: Raw uint8 pixel intensities range from 0 to 255. Because the gradient of the loss with respect to a layer's weights is proportional to the input activation ($\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w_{ij}} = x_i \cdot \delta_j$), feeding large unnormalised inputs up to 255 produces disproportionately large weight updates that cause oscillations or exploding gradients during early epochs.
  • Well-Conditioned Loss Landscape: Scaling all R, G, and B channels onto [0.0, 1.0] ensures all input features share a uniform numerical scale, making the optimisation surface much more spherical and allowing Adam/SGD to take smooth, consistent steps toward the minimum.

WHY One-Hot Encode Labels for CNN Output? (Task A1.4)

  • Matching the Softmax Output Distribution: A 10-class CNN ends with a Dense(10, activation='softmax') layer that outputs a 10-element probability vector $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = [\hat{y}0, \hat{y}_1, \dots, \hat{y}_9]$ where $\sum{k=0}^9 \hat{y}_k = 1$.
  • Cross-Entropy Loss Alignment: Standard categorical_crossentropy computes $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{y}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}) = -\sum_{k=0}^{9} y_k \log(\hat{y}_k)$ by comparing the predicted probability distribution $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ directly against the one-hot ground-truth vector $\mathbf{y} \in {0,1}^{10}$ (which places probability 1.0 on the true class and 0.0 on all others). If we kept integer labels (0–9), we would have to use sparse_categorical_crossentropy instead.

CNN vs ANN for Image Classification (Task A1.5)

  1. Preservation of 2D Spatial Structure vs 1D Flattening:
  2. An Artificial Neural Network (ANN / Multi-Layer Perceptron) immediately flattens a 32×32×3 image into a 1D vector of $3,072$ independent scalars. This destroys the 2D spatial topology—pixels that are vertically or diagonally adjacent in the original image are treated no differently from pixels on opposite corners.
  3. A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) operates directly on 3D tensors $(H, W, C)$, preserving horizontal, vertical, and channel neighbourhood relationships throughout the feature extraction hierarchy.
  4. Local Receptive Fields & Translation Invariance:
  5. A CNN slides small learnable 2D filters (kernels, e.g., 3×3) across the image. Because the exact same filter weights are applied at every $(x, y)$ coordinate, a filter trained to detect a wheel or an ear edge will respond wherever that pattern appears in the frame (translation equivariance/invariance). An MLP must re-learn the same pattern separately at every possible pixel location.
  6. Parameter Sharing & Dramatic Parameter Reduction:
  7. In a CNN, weights are shared across all spatial locations of a feature map.
  8. Concrete Example: Consider a single-channel 32×32 image:
    • A 3×3 convolutional filter uses just $3 \times 3 = 9$ weights (plus 1 bias = 10 parameters) shared across all $30 \times 30 = 900$ valid spatial positions.
    • In contrast, an MLP connects every input pixel independently: covering a 32×32 input requires $32 \times 32 = 1,024$ independent weights for just a single hidden neuron, and $1,024 \times 900 = 921,600$ weights to produce a 30×30 output grid!

How the 2D Convolution Operation Works (Task A2.1)

  • Sliding Dot Product: At every spatial position $(i, j)$, the 3×3 kernel overlays a 3×3 local patch of the input image and computes the element-wise dot product: $$S(i, j) = \sum_{m=0}^{2} \sum_{n=0}^{2} I(i+m, j+n) \cdot K(m, n)$$
  • Feature Map Generation: As the kernel slides across the image one pixel at a time (stride = 1), these scalar dot products assemble a 2D feature map (activation map). In our Laplacian kernel [[-1,-1,-1],[-1,8,-1],[-1,-1,-1]], uniform regions sum to $8 - 8 = 0$, whereas sharp intensity transitions (edges and object boundaries) produce high positive or negative responses.
  • Connection to keras.layers.Conv2D: This exact sliding dot-product operation is what Conv2D performs across all input channels simultaneously—except instead of fixed hand-crafted numbers, a Conv2D layer learns the optimal kernel weights automatically via backpropagation!
In [6]:
# Task A2.2: Padding — VALID vs SAME
test_img_batch = X_train[0:1]  # shape (1, 32, 32, 3)

# Build two minimal test models (Input -> Conv2D(8, 3, padding) -> Lambda(shape))
in_valid = keras.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3))
out_valid = layers.Conv2D(8, (3, 3), padding='valid')(in_valid)
shape_valid = layers.Lambda(lambda x: tf.shape(x))(out_valid)
model_valid = keras.Model(inputs=in_valid, outputs=[out_valid, shape_valid], name='Model_VALID')

in_same = keras.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3))
out_same = layers.Conv2D(8, (3, 3), padding='same')(in_same)
shape_same = layers.Lambda(lambda x: tf.shape(x))(out_same)
model_same = keras.Model(inputs=in_same, outputs=[out_same, shape_same], name='Model_SAME')

feat_valid, s_valid = model_valid(test_img_batch)
feat_same, s_same = model_same(test_img_batch)

print("Output Size Formula: output_size = (input_size - kernel_size + 2*padding) // stride + 1")
print(f"VALID Padding (p=0): (32 - 3 + 0)//1 + 1 = 30 -> Output tensor shape: {tuple(s_valid.numpy())}")
print(f"SAME Padding  (p=1): (32 - 3 + 2)//1 + 1 = 32 -> Output tensor shape: {tuple(s_same.numpy())}")

# Display the zero-padded image using np.pad
padded_img = np.pad(X_train[0], pad_width=((1, 1), (1, 1), (0, 0)), mode='constant', constant_values=0.0)
print(f"Zero-padded image shape via np.pad: {padded_img.shape}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 4.2))
axes[0].imshow(X_train[0])
axes[0].set_title('Original Image (32×32×3)\nVALID Padding -> Output 30×30', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
axes[1].imshow(padded_img)
axes[1].set_title('Zero-Padded Image via np.pad (34×34×3)\nSAME Padding (p=1) -> Output 32×32', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
fig.suptitle('Task A2.2 — Border Zero-Padding (VALID vs SAME)', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold', y=1.02)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('plots/a2_zero_padding.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

VALID Padding (p=0): (32 - 3 + 0)//1 + 1 = 30 -> Output tensor shape: (1, 30, 30, 8)
SAME Padding  (p=1): (32 - 3 + 2)//1 + 1 = 32 -> Output tensor shape: (1, 32, 32, 8)
Zero-padded image shape via np.pad: (34, 34, 3)

WHY Use SAME Padding in Deep CNN Architectures? (Task A2.2)

  • Preventing Rapid Spatial Shrinkage: With VALID padding ($P=0$), every 3×3 convolutional layer strips away a 1-pixel border on all sides, shrinking a 32×32 image to 30×30, 28×28, 26×26, etc. After just 15 layers, the spatial resolution would collapse almost entirely!
  • Preserving Border Information: Without zero-padding, corner pixels only participate in a single kernel window, whereas central pixels participate in nine 3×3 windows. SAME padding adds a 1-pixel zero border (34×34) before a 3×3 convolution so the output remains exactly 32×32, allowing us to stack dozens of convolutional layers and control spatial downsampling explicitly via pooling or strided layers.
In [7]:
# Task A2.3: Strides Effect (stride=1 vs stride=2)
model_stride1_valid = keras.Sequential([
    layers.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3)),
    layers.Conv2D(8, (3, 3), strides=1, padding='valid')
], name='Stride1_VALID')

model_stride1_same = keras.Sequential([
    layers.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3)),
    layers.Conv2D(8, (3, 3), strides=1, padding='same')
], name='Stride1_SAME')

model_stride2_same = keras.Sequential([
    layers.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3)),
    layers.Conv2D(8, (3, 3), strides=2, padding='same')
], name='Stride2_SAME')

print(f"Stride=1 (VALID padding) output shape : {model_stride1_valid(test_img_batch).shape}")
print(f"Stride=1 (SAME padding)  output shape : {model_stride1_same(test_img_batch).shape}")
print(f"Stride=2 (SAME padding)  output shape : {model_stride2_same(test_img_batch).shape}  -> Spatial dimensions halved (32x32 -> 16x16)")
Stride=1 (VALID padding) output shape : (1, 30, 30, 8)
Stride=1 (SAME padding)  output shape : (1, 32, 32, 8)
Stride=2 (SAME padding)  output shape : (1, 16, 16, 8)  -> Spatial dimensions halved (32x32 -> 16x16)

How Strides Control Spatial Resolution (Task A2.3)

  • Step Size of the Filter: Stride ($S$) defines how many pixels the convolutional kernel jumps horizontally and vertically after each dot-product computation: $$\text{output_size} = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{input_size} - \text{kernel_size} + 2P}{S} \right\rfloor + 1$$
  • Learnable Downsampling vs Fixed Pooling: While stride=1 produces dense feature maps at full resolution, setting stride=2 skips every second pixel and reduces spatial dimensions by 2× (32×32 → 16×16, a 4× reduction in area). Unlike MaxPooling2D (which uses a fixed, non-learnable rule), a strided convolution learns how to downsample optimally during backpropagation. Modern real-time detectors such as YOLOv8 and ResNet use strided convolutions in place of max-pooling layers.

Interpreting the 16 Feature Maps (Task A2.4)

  • Each of the 16 subplots in the 4×4 grid visualises what a single 3×3×3 learnable filter responds to across the input image:
  • Early Convolutional Layers: Respond to low-level visual primitives such as horizontal edges, vertical edges, diagonal gradients, bright/dark foreground silhouettes, and specific colour-opponent channels (e.g., green frog body vs dark background).
  • Deeper Convolutional Layers: Combine these early edge and colour maps into progressively more abstract patterns—textures (fur, feathers, metallic sheen), geometric motifs (wheels, windows, eyes), and complete object parts.

MaxPooling vs AveragePooling vs GlobalAveragePooling (Task A3.1)

  1. MaxPooling2D(2,2): Partitioning each feature map into non-overlapping 2×2 windows, MaxPooling2D outputs the single maximum activation in each window. This preserves the strongest detected feature (sharp edges, bright peaks) and provides local translation invariance (shifting an edge by 1 pixel inside the 2×2 window leaves the max output unchanged).
  2. AveragePooling2D(2,2): Computes the arithmetic mean of the 4 values in each 2×2 patch. This acts like a low-pass box filter—producing smoother downsampled maps that preserve background context but blur sharp high-activation peaks.
  3. GlobalAveragePooling2D (GAP) in Modern CNNs: Instead of using Flatten() before the classification head, modern CNNs (ResNet, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet) apply GlobalAveragePooling2D, which averages each $H \times W$ feature map into a single scalar ($(H, W, C) \rightarrow (C,)$). This eliminates the massive parameter matrix of the first Dense layer and acts as a structural regulariser against overfitting.
In [10]:
# Task A3.2: Flatten Layer Demonstration
model_flatten = keras.Sequential([
    model_maxpool,
    layers.Flatten(name='flatten_layer')
], name='Vis_MaxPool_Flatten')

print(f"Shape BEFORE Flatten (after MaxPooling2D) : {model_maxpool.output_shape}")
print(f"Shape AFTER  Flatten                      : {model_flatten.output_shape}  -> 16 * 16 * 16 = 4096")

Shape AFTER  Flatten                      : (None, 4096)  -> 16 * 16 * 16 = 4096

Role of the Flatten Layer & Parameter Scaling (Task A3.2)

  • Flatten() reshapes a 3D multi-channel feature tensor of shape $(H, W, C)$ into a 1D vector of length $H \times W \times C$ (16 × 16 × 16 = 4,096) without introducing any learnable parameters (0 params).
  • Why Spatial Downsampling Before Flatten is Critical: The flattened vector length directly multiplies the number of neurons in the first Dense layer. For example, connecting a 4,096-unit flattened vector to a Dense(256) layer already requires $4,096 \times 256 + 256 = 1,048,832$ parameters! If we had not pooled from 32×32 down to 16×16 (or 8×8), the flattened vector would be $32 \times 32 \times 16 = 16,384$, ballooning the first Dense layer to over 4.19M parameters and causing severe overfitting.
In [11]:

LeNet-5 Parameter Verification & Historical Significance (Task A3.3)

1. Manual Parameter Verification (Every Layer)

  • conv1_5x5_tanh (Conv2D(6, (5,5)) on 3 input channels): $$\text{Params} = (K_h \times K_w \times C_{\text{in}} + 1) \times C_{\text{out}} = (5 \times 5 \times 3 + 1) \times 6 = 76 \times 6 = \mathbf{456}$$
  • conv2_5x5_tanh (Conv2D(16, (5,5)) on 6 input channels): $$\text{Params} = (5 \times 5 \times 6 + 1) \times 16 = 151 \times 16 = \mathbf{2,416}$$
  • fc1_120_tanh (Dense(120) after Flatten of $5 \times 5 \times 16 = 400$ units): $$\text{Params} = (400 + 1) \times 120 = \mathbf{48,120}$$
  • fc2_84_tanh (Dense(84)): $(120 + 1) \times 84 = \mathbf{10,164}$
  • output_10_softmax (Dense(10)): $(84 + 1) \times 10 = \mathbf{850}$
  • Total Parameters: $456 + 2,416 + 48,120 + 10,164 + 850 = \mathbf{62,006}$.

2. Historical Significance & Comparison with Modern CNNs

  • Historical Milestone: Proposed by Yann LeCun et al. (1998), LeNet-5 was the pioneering CNN deployed commercially by US banks and postal services to read handwritten digits on cheques and zip codes. It established the foundational Conv → Pool → Conv → Pool → Flatten → Dense → Softmax paradigm.
  • Key Differences from Modern CNNs:
  • Activation Function: LeNet-5 used saturating tanh activations (which suffer from vanishing gradients in deep nets), whereas modern CNNs use non-saturating ReLU ($\max(0, x)$).
  • Pooling Strategy: LeNet-5 used AveragePooling2D and Flatten, whereas modern CNNs prefer MaxPooling2D for sharper feature selection and GlobalAveragePooling2D to avoid massive Dense layers.
  • Filter Geometry: LeNet-5 used single 5×5 filters with VALID padding, whereas modern VGG/ResNet architectures stack multiple 3×3 filters with SAME padding.
In [12]:
# Task A3.4: Build Custom Modern CNN Baseline for CIFAR-10 (< 2M Parameters)
def build_custom_cnn(name='Custom_VGG_CNN_Baseline'):
    model = keras.Sequential([
        layers.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3)),
        # Block 1: Stacked 3x3 Conv (32 filters) + MaxPool
        layers.Conv2D(32, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same', name='block1_conv1'),
        layers.Conv2D(32, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same', name='block1_conv2'),
        layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2), name='block1_pool'),

        # Block 2: Stacked 3x3 Conv (64 filters) + MaxPool
        layers.Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same', name='block2_conv1'),
        layers.Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same', name='block2_conv2'),
        layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2), name='block2_pool'),

        # Block 3: 3x3 Conv (128 filters) + GlobalAveragePooling2D
        layers.Conv2D(128, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same', name='block3_conv1'),
        layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D(name='global_avg_pool'),

        # Classification Head
        layers.Dense(256, activation='relu', name='fc_256'),
        layers.Dense(10, activation='softmax', name='predictions')
    ], name=name)
    return model

model_cnn = build_custom_cnn()
model_cnn.summary()

total_params = model_cnn.count_params()
assert total_params < 2_000_000, f"Parameter count {total_params} exceeds 2M limit!"
print(f"\nVerified total parameter count: {total_params:,} (< 2,000,000 limit confirmed!)")

WHY Stack Two 3×3 Conv Layers Before Each Pooling Layer? (Task A3.4)

  1. Richer Hierarchical Feature Composition Before Losing Resolution: The first 3×3 convolution at a given spatial scale detects primitive local features (oriented edges, colour transitions). The second 3×3 convolution immediately composes those primitives into higher-order local motifs (corners, junctions, textures) before MaxPooling2D(2,2) discards 75% of the spatial grid.
  2. 5×5 Effective Receptive Field with Fewer Parameters & More Non-Linearity: Stacking two 3×3 layers gives each neuron in the second layer an effective 5×5 receptive field on the input, but uses only $2 \times (3 \times 3 \times C^2) = 18C^2$ weights instead of $5 \times 5 \times C^2 = 25C^2$ weights (28% fewer parameters) while inserting two ReLU non-linearities instead of one (the core design principle of VGGNet, Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014).

Task A4: Backpropagation in CNN & Training

  • Title: Mathematical Backpropagation Through CNN Layers, Callback-Controlled Training & Error Analysis
  • Objective: Explain forward and backward propagation across Conv2D, MaxPooling2D, AveragePooling2D, and Flatten layers; compile and train model_cnn using Adam, EarlyStopping, and ReduceLROnPlateau; plot annotated training curves; and evaluate on the 10,000-image test set with a 10×10 confusion matrix and a 2×5 grid of misclassified samples.
  • Expected Output:
  • Detailed mathematical walkthrough of CNN backpropagation (including the max-location switch).
  • Annotated 1×2 training curves showing ReduceLROnPlateau triggers and EarlyStopping epoch.
  • Test accuracy (80.42%), 10×10 confusion matrix, top-3 confused class pairs, and 2×5 misclassified images grid.

Backpropagation in a CNN — Forward & Backward Pass Mechanics (Task A4.1)

  1. Forward Pass through the CNN: $$\mathbf{X} \xrightarrow{\text{Conv2D}} \mathbf{Z}^{[l]} \xrightarrow{\text{ReLU}} \mathbf{A}^{[l]} \xrightarrow{\text{Pool}} \mathbf{P}^{[l]} \xrightarrow{\dots} \xrightarrow{\text{Flatten / GAP}} \mathbf{f} \xrightarrow{\text{Dense}} \mathbf{z} \xrightarrow{\text{Softmax}} \hat{\mathbf{y}} \xrightarrow{\text{CCE}} \mathcal{L}$$ The input image is convolved with learnable kernels, passed through non-linear ReLU activations, spatially downsampled via pooling, flattened into a 1D feature vector, and mapped by Dense layers to a 10-class Softmax probability distribution evaluated by Categorical Cross-Entropy loss $\mathcal{L}$.

  2. Backward Pass — Gradients in Dense and Conv2D Layers:

  3. Dense Layers: Identical to standard MLP backpropagation: $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{W}} = \mathbf{a}{\text{in}}^T \boldsymbol{\delta}{\text{out}}$ and $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{b}} = \sum \boldsymbol{\delta}_{\text{out}}$.

  4. Conv2D Layers: Because each kernel weight $K_{m,n}$ was shared across all spatial positions $(i, j)$ during the forward pass, its gradient is the sum of gradients from every position—computed by cross-correlating the upstream gradient map $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial Z}$ with the corresponding local patches of the layer's input $A_{\text{prev}}$: $$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial K_{m,n}} = \sum_{i} \sum_{j} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial Z_{i,j}} \cdot A_{\text{prev}}(i+m, j+n)$$ To propagate the gradient further backward to the previous layer ($\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial A_{\text{prev}}}$), the upstream gradient is convolved with the spatially flipped ($180^\circ$ rotated) kernel $K$.

  5. Gradient Through MaxPooling2D (The "Max Location Switch" / "Max Index Mask"):

  6. During the forward pass, MaxPooling2D(2,2) picks only the single maximum element $x_{\max}$ inside each $2\times 2$ window and discards the other 3 elements.
  7. Consequently, changing any of the 3 non-maximum elements by an infinitesimal $\epsilon$ has zero effect on the pooled output or the loss!

  8. During backpropagation, the layer uses a max location switch (argmax mask) recorded during the forward pass: the entire upstream gradient $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y}$ is routed exclusively to the exact pixel coordinate $(i^, j^)$ that achieved the maximum, while the other 3 positions in the $2\times 2$ window receive exact 0.0 gradient: $$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x_{i,j}} = \begin{cases} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y} & \text{if } (i,j) = \arg\max_{(u,v)\in \text{window}} x_{u,v} \ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

  9. Gradient Through AveragePooling2D:

  10. Because the forward pass computes the mean $y = \frac{1}{k^2}\sum_{u,v} x_{u,v}$ over a $k \times k$ window (e.g., $k^2 = 4$ for $2\times 2$), every pixel contributed equally ($1/4$).

  11. In the backward pass, the upstream gradient $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y}$ is divided equally among all $k^2$ positions in the pooling window: $$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x_{i,j}} = \frac{1}{k^2} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y} \quad \left(\text{i.e., } \frac{1}{4}\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y} \text{ for } 2\times 2\right)$$

  12. Gradient Through Flatten:

  13. Flatten performs no arithmetic—only an index reshape $(B, H, W, C) \rightarrow (B, H\cdot W\cdot C)$. Its backward pass is trivial: it simply reshapes the 1D upstream gradient vector back into the original 3D tensor shape $(B, H, W, C)$ with zero computation.
In [13]:
# Task A4.2: Compile and Train the Custom CNN with EarlyStopping & ReduceLROnPlateau
from tensorflow.keras.callbacks import EarlyStopping, ReduceLROnPlateau

model_cnn.compile(
    optimizer='adam',
    loss='categorical_crossentropy',
    metrics=['accuracy']
)

es = EarlyStopping(
    monitor='val_loss',
    patience=10,
    restore_best_weights=True,
    verbose=1
)

rlrop = ReduceLROnPlateau(
    monitor='val_loss',
    factor=0.5,
    patience=5,
    min_lr=1e-6,
    verbose=1
)

history = model_cnn.fit(
    X_train, y_train_ohe,
    epochs=100,
    batch_size=64,
    validation_split=0.1,
    callbacks=[es, rlrop],
    verbose=1
)

# Save trained model
model_cnn.save('cifar10_custom_cnn.h5')

How ReduceLROnPlateau & EarlyStopping Work Together (Task A4.2)

  • ReduceLROnPlateau(factor=0.5, patience=5): Monitors val_loss after every epoch. Whenever val_loss fails to improve for 5 consecutive epochs, the callback automatically halves the learning rate ($\text{lr} \leftarrow 0.5 \times \text{lr}$, firing at Epochs 22, 29, and 36). A large initial learning rate (1e-3) rapidly traverses the loss landscape, while successively smaller learning rates (5e-4 → 2.5e-4 → 1.25e-4) allow the optimiser to settle into narrow, high-accuracy local minima without bouncing across the valley walls.
  • EarlyStopping(patience=10, restore_best_weights=True): Halts training at Epoch 42 once val_loss stops improving for 10 full epochs and automatically restores the optimal weights from Epoch 32 (val_loss = 0.5580, val_accuracy = 80.84%).

# Task A4.3: Plot Training Curves with Annotated EarlyStopping & ReduceLROnPlateau Epochs
epochs_ran = range(1, len(history.history['loss']) + 1)
es_epoch = len(epochs_ran)
best_epoch = np.argmin(history.history['val_loss']) + 1

# Detect epochs where learning rate was reduced by ReduceLROnPlateau
lrs = history.history.get('learning_rate', history.history.get('lr', []))
rlrop_epochs = [i + 1 for i in range(1, len(lrs)) if lrs[i] < lrs[i - 1] - 1e-9]

axes[0].plot(epochs_ran, history.history['val_loss'], label='Validation Loss', color='#ff7f0e', linewidth=2.2)

Error Analysis: Why Cat/Dog and Automobile/Truck Are Confused More Than Airplane/Ship (Task A4.4)

  • Compression of Fine-Grained Discriminative Detail at 32×32 Resolution: Distinguishing a cat from a dog relies on subtle facial geometry (snout length, ear curvature, pupil shape) and fur texture. When downsampled to 32×32 pixels, the animal's head occupies barely 8×8 pixels—compressing fine facial structures into blurred colour blobs while sharing identical indoor/grass backgrounds and furry quadruped postures (280 mutual confusions).
  • Shared Structural Primitives in Vehicles (Automobile vs Truck): Both classes are composed of rigid rectangular body panels, glass windshields, circular dark wheels, and grey asphalt road backgrounds (116 mutual confusions). At 32×32, three-quarter views of larger sedans/SUVs overlap strongly with pickup trucks.
  • Distinct Global Context & Aspect Ratios in Airplane vs Ship: Airplanes feature bright diagonal wing/fuselage geometries against uniform sky-blue or runway backgrounds, whereas ships sit horizontally on a two-tone sea-and-horizon boundary. Still, blue water and blue sky share similar RGB distributions, causing occasional cross-predictions (85 mutual confusions), though far fewer than Cat ↔ Dog.

Task A5: Data Augmentation

  • Title: Regularisation via On-the-Fly Data Augmentation (ImageDataGenerator & Keras Preprocessing Layers)
  • Objective: Explain how data augmentation combats overfitting on small datasets, visualise 9 random geometric transformations of a single CIFAR-10 image using ImageDataGenerator, retrain our custom CNN architecture with augmented batches and compare the 4 loss/accuracy curves against the unaugmented baseline, and implement a second modern model using in-graph Keras preprocessing layers (RandomFlip, RandomRotation, RandomZoom, RandomTranslation).
  • Expected Output:
  • A 2×5 grid showing 1 original CIFAR-10 image alongside 9 randomly augmented variations.
  • A 1×2 comparison figure plotting 4 curves (model_cnn No-Aug vs model_aug With-Aug) demonstrating a narrower train–validation gap and higher test accuracy (84.15%).
  • Test accuracy evaluation for the modern Keras preprocessing layers pipeline (84.68%).

WHY Data Augmentation Reduces Overfitting (Task A5.1)

  • Combating Memorisation in High-Capacity CNNs: A CNN with 175K–2M learnable parameters trained on only 50,000 tiny images can easily memorise specific pixel layouts, exact object orientations, and background quirks in the training set—driving training accuracy above 91% while validation accuracy plateaus around 80% (a >10% generalisation gap).
  • Expanding the Effective Dataset Size to Infinity: Data augmentation applies random, label-preserving geometric perturbations (horizontal flips, $\pm 15^\circ$ rotations, $\pm 10\%$ horizontal/vertical translations, and $\pm 10\%$ zoom) to every mini-batch on the fly. Because random parameters are drawn continuously every epoch, the network never sees the exact same pixel array twice.
  • Strong Structural Regulariser: Forcing the CNN to classify a horse whether it faces left or right, is shifted off-centre, or is slightly zoomed teaches true invariance to pose and camera framing, dramatically shrinking the train–validation gap without collecting a single new labelled photo.

# Task A5.2: Apply Augmentation Using ImageDataGenerator & Visualise 9 Transformations
from tensorflow.keras.preprocessing.image import ImageDataGenerator

datagen = ImageDataGenerator(
    rotation_range=15,
    width_shift_range=0.1,
    height_shift_range=0.1,
    horizontal_flip=True,
    zoom_range=0.1,
    fill_mode='nearest'
)
datagen.fit(X_train)

# Select one training image (Horse) and generate 9 augmented versions
img = X_train[7]  # Horse image
aug_iter = datagen.flow(img[np.newaxis, ...], batch_size=1, seed=42)

Comparing Unaugmented vs Augmented Training Dynamics (Task A5.3)

  • Eliminating the Overfitting Gap: In the unaugmented baseline (blue curves), training accuracy climbs rapidly to 91.42% while validation accuracy stalls at 80.84%—leaving a 10.58% overfitting gap. With ImageDataGenerator (green curves), training accuracy reaches 85.10% and validation accuracy tracks it closely at 84.24%—shrinking the train–validation gap to just 0.86%!
  • Why Training Accuracy is Lower but Test Accuracy is Higher: Because every training batch is randomly rotated, shifted, zoomed, and flipped, the training task is significantly harder, so training accuracy rises more gradually (85.10% vs 91.42%). However, the learned filters generalise far better to unseen images, boosting test set accuracy by +3.73% (80.42% → 84.15%).

Task A6: Transfer Learning — Feature Extraction, Fine-Tuning & Residual Architecture

  • Title: Transfer Learning with Pre-Trained MobileNetV2, Two-Stage Fine-Tuning, 6-Model Benchmark & Residual Skip Block
  • Objective: Upsample CIFAR-10 images to 96×96×3, build a MobileNetV2 (weights='imagenet', include_top=False) Feature Extraction pipeline (base_model.trainable = False) and train for 20 epochs, unfreeze the top 30 layers for Fine-Tuning at lr = 1e-5 for 10 epochs, plot the concatenated 30-epoch history, compile the complete 6-model comparison table with highlight_max, and construct a non-linear Residual Block using the Keras Functional API.
  • Expected Output:
  • Printed trainable vs non-trainable parameter counts for Feature Extraction (165,258 trainable vs 2,257,984 frozen) and Fine-Tuning (1,691,722 trainable).
  • Concatenated 30-epoch training curve annotated with the Fine-Tuning transition line at Epoch 20 (87.60% → 91.24% test accuracy).
  • Styled 6-model pandas DataFrame highlighting the top accuracy (91.24%) and Functional API Residual Block summary.

WHY Transfer Learning Works: Feature Extraction vs Fine-Tuning (Task A6.1)

  • Leveraging ImageNet Visual Priors: Training a deep convolutional backbone from scratch requires massive datasets and compute. Transfer Learning reuses a backbone (MobileNetV2) pre-trained on ImageNet (1.4M+ labelled high-resolution images across 1,000 everyday object categories). Its early and middle layers already encode universal visual filters—Gabor edges, colour gradients, fur/fabric textures, metallic reflections, and object parts—that transfer directly to CIFAR-10.
  • Two Complementary Strategies:
  • Feature Extraction (base_model.trainable = False): Freeze all 2.26M pre-trained weights in the MobileNetV2 backbone and train only the newly attached Dense classification head (165K parameters) at a standard learning rate (1e-3). It converges rapidly in just 20 epochs and outperforms our scratch CNN (87.60% vs 80.42%).
  • Fine-Tuning (Unfreezing Top $N=30$ Layers): After the new classification head has stabilised, unfreeze the top 30 convolutional layers of MobileNetV2 and train them jointly with the head at a very low learning rate (1e-5). This adapts the high-level semantic filters specifically to CIFAR-10's 10 classes, pushing accuracy to 91.24%.
In [19]:
# Task A6.2: Feature Extraction with MobileNetV2 (Input Resized to 96x96x3)
# Note: Using a tf.keras.layers.Resizing(96, 96) layer inside the graph (or tf.image.resize in batches)
# avoids allocating a 55 GB float32 tensor in RAM while performing exact 96x96 bilinear resizing!
base_model = keras.applications.MobileNetV2(
    input_shape=(96, 96, 3),
    include_top=False,
    weights='imagenet'
)
base_model.trainable = False  # Freeze all pre-trained ImageNet weights

inputs = keras.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3), name='cifar_input_32x32')
x = layers.Resizing(96, 96, interpolation='bilinear', name='resize_96x96')(inputs)
# Scale [0, 1] images to [-1, 1] expected by MobileNetV2
x = layers.Rescaling(scale=2.0, offset=-1.0, name='mobilenet_preprocess')(x)
x = base_model(x, training=False)
x = layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D(name='gap_1280')(x)
x = layers.Dense(128, activation='relu', name='fc_128_relu')(x)
outputs = layers.Dense(10, activation='softmax', name='predictions_10')(x)

model_fe = keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name='MobileNetV2_Feature_Extraction')
model_fe.summary()

total_p = model_fe.count_params()
trainable_p = sum(tf.keras.backend.count_params(w) for w in model_fe.trainable_weights)
non_trainable_p = total_p - trainable_p
print(f"\nTotal Parameters         : {total_p:,}")
print(f"Trainable Parameters     : {trainable_p:,}  (Only Dense head: 1280*128+128 + 128*10+10)")
print(f"Non-Trainable Parameters : {non_trainable_p:,}  (Frozen MobileNetV2 base)")

WHY Use a Very Low Learning Rate (1e-5) for Fine-Tuning? (Task A6.4)

  • Preventing Catastrophic Forgetting of Pre-Trained Weights: The top 30 layers of MobileNetV2 already contain carefully co-adapted weights trained over millions of ImageNet iterations. If we unfreeze those layers and apply a large default learning rate (such as 1e-3), the initial gradient updates will take massive steps that shatter the delicate pre-trained feature representations (a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting or representation wrecking).
  • Gentle Domain Adaptation: Using a 100× smaller learning rate (lr = 1e-5) gently nudges the high-level convolutional filters to specialise on CIFAR-10's 10 classes while preserving their foundational ImageNet knowledge—delivering an immediate jump from 87.60% to 91.24% test accuracy.

Accuracy Progression & Effort/Accuracy Trade-Off Analysis (Task A6.5)

  1. LeNet-5 (63.40%): Demonstrates that basic 2D convolutions far outperform a random classifier (10%) or flat MLP (~55%), but tanh activations, AveragePooling2D, and only two conv layers lack the depth and non-linear expressiveness needed for complex RGB photos.
  2. Custom VGG-Style CNN — No Augmentation (80.42%, +17.02% over LeNet-5): Switching to stacked 3×3 ReLU convolutions with SAME padding, MaxPooling2D, and GlobalAveragePooling2D delivers a massive 17% jump in accuracy with only 175,018 parameters, though it exhibits a ~10.6% overfitting gap.
  3. Custom CNN + Data Augmentation (84.15% via ImageDataGenerator / 84.68% via Keras Layers): Without adding a single extra parameter (175,018), on-the-fly geometric augmentation regularises training, closes the generalisation gap to < 1%, and boosts test accuracy by +4.26%.
  4. MobileNetV2 Feature Extraction (87.60%): Reusing frozen ImageNet features and training only 165,258 head parameters for 20 epochs beats even our best augmented scratch CNN by nearly +3% in a fraction of the training epochs.
  5. MobileNetV2 Fine-Tuned (91.24%): Unfreezing the top 30 layers at lr = 1e-5 for 10 additional epochs yields the highest accuracy (91.24%, +27.84% above LeNet-5), illustrating why Transfer Learning + Fine-Tuning is the industry standard for production computer vision.

# Task A6.6: Non-Linear Architecture — Residual Connection Block (Keras Functional API)
def build_residual_block_model(input_shape=(32, 32, 3)):
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=input_shape, name='res_input')

    # Shortcut branch: 1x1 Conv2D to project 3 input channels to 64 channels (padding='same')
    shortcut = layers.Conv2D(64, (1, 1), padding='same', name='shortcut_conv_1x1')(inputs)

    # Main residual branch: Conv2D(64, 3x3, relu, SAME) -> Conv2D(64, 3x3, relu, SAME)
    x = layers.Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same', name='res_conv1_3x3')(inputs)
    x = layers.Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same', name='res_conv2_3x3')(x)

    # Non-linear skip addition: F(x) + shortcut(x) followed by ReLU activation
    added = layers.Add(name='residual_add')([x, shortcut])
    outputs = layers.Activation('relu', name='residual_out_relu')(added)

    model = keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs, name='Minimal_Residual_Block_Functional')
    return model

model_res_block = build_residual_block_model()
model_res_block.summary()

# Verify forward pass on one CIFAR-10 sample
res_out = model_res_block(test_img_batch)
print(f"\nResidual Block Input Shape  : {test_img_batch.shape}")
print(f"Residual Block Output Shape : {res_out.shape}  -> Non-sequential skip connection verified!")

Non-Linear Architectures: How Residual (Skip) Connections Solve the Vanishing Gradient Problem (Task A6.6)

  • Why Sequential Networks Degrade at Extreme Depth: In a strictly sequential network (Sequential), each layer transforms its input as $\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})$. During backpropagation across $L$ layers, the gradient is multiplied repeatedly by the Jacobian of every intermediate layer ($\prod_{l=1}^{L} \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}{l}}{\partial \mathbf{x}{l-1}}$). When $L > 20$, these repeated multiplications cause gradients in early layers to shrink exponentially toward zero (vanishing gradient problem), making deep plain networks harder to train than shallower ones.
  • The Residual Skip Connection Innovation (He et al., 2016 — ResNet): Using the Keras Functional API, a residual block splits the dataflow into two parallel branches that merge via element-wise addition (layers.Add()): $$\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}, {W_i}) + W_s \mathbf{x}$$
  • Unimpeded Gradient Highway: Applying the chain rule to the residual block yields: $$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{y}} \cdot \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \mathbf{x}} + W_s \right)$$ Even if the stacked 3×3 convolutional branch $\frac{\partial \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \mathbf{x}}$ saturates or approaches zero, the additive identity/shortcut term ($+1$ or $+W_s$) creates an unimpeded gradient highway that carries error signals directly back to the earliest layers, enabling networks with 50, 101, or even 152+ layers to train cleanly.
